blocks.x: Let's see, we're interviewing today at Katie's in Liberty.
Could I have the exact address, Ms. Ivor? 2238 Katie's.
2238 Katie's. And today is November... 17th? November the 17th, huh? Wednesday.
And let's get everybody's name down. It's 1959. Yeah, 1959. What's that? Okay, Punch, let's get your name down there.
Ernest Miller.
And can we get your name?
We want your name. What's my name? Yeah.
And what does everybody call you? What does everybody call you? What does everybody call me?
Somebody call me Little Dad and Charlie sometimes. I'm calling him a bandit player and he's called a Little Dad.
And I'm Dick Allen. My name's Paul Crawford. Could we get your name down too, Ms. Ivor?
We're running down too. See?
Good. And how you feeling, Dan? I'm feeling... I'm feeling...
I'm feeling bad now. Oh, that's it. I'm feeling bad now. Oh, that's it. I'm feeling bad now.
Oh, that's it.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
How long?
Oh, how long? I play sheet music? No. Okay. Public? Public shop. Oh, how many pieces? Oh, how many people? How many people? How many people? You know? P-E-E.
Publish.
Oh, publish. How many you mean? How long? Oh, how long?
Did you make it? You know, did you help them with the sheet music?
Tulane and Levin. With the two pieces? Sheet music. On Tulane. Oh, Tulane you mean? Yeah, so how long did you help them sell the music? On Tulane Avenue. Let me see. Tulane Avenue.
Tell them, P-Ron and Williams.

P-Ron and Williams. Oh, you mean how long did I? Oh, I didn't play with them then. They used to go there, you know. And when we'd go off, well he'd give me a stack of music to sell, you know. He'd go to the streets, folks, and Texas, all them places, and Oklahoma, you know. And he'd give me a bunch like that to sell for, you know. But I wasn't at the place, I just used to go there sometime. I wasn't playing with him then, you know. I played with him after they'd get that up, him and Clarence William, you know. Clarence William had left there, you know.
How did you sell that music?
How did you sell that music? How did I sell it? Ten cents a copper.
At homes or at parties or what? In the home or at a party or?

You see, at the home or in a party or how? That's on the street you sell it? No, anywhere we go, you see. People come up to the band, you know. I ask them if they want to buy a piece. And a whole lot of musicians used to come. So we used to sell as a musician a ten cents a copper. And the other people was fifteen cents, you know. Them would want to play it on the piano. You know, they entertained itself. I used to sell them too.
When did he go to Mexico? Ask him about that trip.

So when did you go to Mexico? I went to Mexico in 1926. I stayed over there three months and a half. I paid with a white band over there. I paid with a 110. Professor Connett, that's what his name was. And I got scared of him. I thought I couldn't hear the word. But I'm sure were the places where he was the same thing. I'd say, I'd say, they're the same as A, B, C, D, you know. But I got along good with him. I played with him about twice over there. Then I played with another little four piece band over there. Just all little jobs, you know, paid with him. But my band wasn't doing nothing. Whose band was that? Whose band was that in Mexico? It was Charlie Toad. You know what I mean? From your hand. Charlie Toad. He carried us over there. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.
Mm-hm. Mm-hm.

Mm-hm. back there about three months and he died. He went over with us too. Red Island, you see him over there, we used to play together, yeah. That's when I went to Mexico. I cut him to go to Mexico and he told me when I come back my job would be there for me. So when I come back we went together. I couldn't get him to go nowhere. So I threw out here with Faith Martin and then he went to send him to come back. Then he had a break and go to New York. He's been gone ever since.
Ask him did he know Joe Oliver?

Did you know Joe Oliver? Oh yeah, Joe. He was on the corner from Joe Oliver. That's the time I used to go to the Royal Guard. He got that job out today. Bless you know. Yeah, he was the king out there. And then when he was older than me, he was about five or six years old than me. But I know them when they first had a band organized. There was a brother named Kintin. He had all these youngsters from fifteen to eighteen years old playing a bass band. He used to carry them all around in different places up and down the country. Then when they come back there, Joe got good. Then Joe, she just made up a band himself. And everybody played with him. The first lick I hit on the guitar was Joe, Joe, Oliver and old man Umphrey. He stayed in California a long time too. The Clown-Eyed player. The Clown-Eyed player. Yeah, Clown-Eyed player. And we was passing there by the plate. I couldn't go in the ball. It was a body there. If they happened to slip me in. And they say, you reckon you can play a piece in it? I said, I tried to play something new. I said, play the blues. They played the blues. I played. And that sucked me playing with a band after that, you know.
Who was in that band? Kinkins Band or Jenkins?
Who was in that band? Jenkins. Jenkins. Jenkins.
He was talking about the Kid Band with Joe Oliver.
Joe Oliver. Oh. Joe Oliver, oh. The only one I can know is uh, uh, uh, that's part of the name Rob Palmer. Mm-hmm. Cimbone player. Is he up there yet?
He's in Chicago.

Oh, Chicago. They had him, Hellman Umphrey on the, on the Clown-Eyed. He said, he had a bass. And he said, it was old time fellas. I can't remember them, you know, when he first started out. And then when he left here, he left here with a bunch of fellas from here, you know. Then he sent to Lewis Armstrong. And I said, they stayed together. But he was still living around the corner from here. On the street. And then when his wife come back, after she died, she come right back there, and they're there about six months. And then she moved, you know.
Well, she's on Phillip Street now. On Phillip Street?
Stella.
Yeah. Stella Oliver is on Phillip Street now. Oh, yeah. She lives right near John Casimir. Oh, yeah. I see her once in a while. Yeah.
Let's see.
Oh, we didn't get her by Charlie Tolles' band. Who was in Charlie Tolles' band? Who was in Charlie Tolles' band?

Who was in Charlie Tolles' band? Oh, me. At the age. And a fella named, this fella I'll tell you about Moran. And a fella named Johnson. And see, he had his wife playing piano. And a fella playing Clowness named Johnson. So, we, we killed a rotten band over there. You see, it wasn't our fault. Charlie Tolles had his band. And when they said he was going to Mexico, well, his band backed out. And he just had to grab anybody he could get to go. So, he got I-Ted and my-Ted got me. And then my-Ted got the, uh, the cornet player. And he got the saxophone money. They were just learning. But Johnson was an old cornet player. But he never was much, you know. What did Tolles play? Tolles, he was playing bass. And he could play trumpet too. And he just could play trumpet alike, you know. As most of he was playing bass. And what did Octave play then? Drum then. And I played drum and piano. And then he had his wife playing piano. And his wife was a good musician but she couldn't play with the band. And all they were doing was making motions, you know. And he had to take a piece by herself and sing. This was a good song for her, you know. She could sing like that. Sometimes, I tell you, they had to double up and play the piano, you know. With us when we was over there. And sometimes they mixed up with the Mexican band. They played with us sometimes. All them over there was holler on that string instrument. They used to give me $10 to learn that wrist. I had so much wrist, you know. Like that. And they liked that wrist, you know. And I was going like that. And holler didn't get that. And we carried the Charleston over there too, you know. The Charleston dance wasn't there. We carried that over there.
Ask him who danced the Charleston. Who danced it? Yeah, over there in Mexico.

Say, who danced the Charleston over there in Mexico? Who's taking us over there? Who danced the Charleston? Who's that boy's name? Pete. I don't know, Pete. I can put my pictures in there. I'd like to see him. Someday. Not now. We can get him in a minute. Yeah, do that in a box here. We'll be all right after you get that dog. Oh, what? What? What? What? What? What?
What?
What? What? What? What?
What?
What? What? What? What? What? What? What?
What? What?
What?
What?
What? What? What? What?
What? What? What? What?
What? On guitar, I must have been about twenty-two years, twenty-one, twenty-two. They were starting on guitar.
And when did he change the banjo?

And when did you change the banjo? Let me see. I must have stayed on guitar about five years. And then they, not that long, about two years. And then they come out with the banjo. And I didn't want to change. Me and Janice received. We said we wasn't going to change. And that was the only man I had to meet to see who was the best. And when I did meet him, we played, couldn't tell him who was the best. They said we played the same way, same style. He's back over there now, up in the North, somewhere. Los Angeles, isn't he? Isn't he in Los Angeles? Who? Sincere. Say he did what? I said, don't he live in Los Angeles? Yeah, that's right.
California. California. California.
Oh yeah, yeah, that's right, California.
He's even thinking of starting to play the string bass. Yeah.

George Foster. You know him, don't you? Bass player. And he had a brother named, uh, Willie. Charlie! Willie, yeah. White fella. Yeah, yeah. I know him. Because he'd play violin, and he'd get up a violin once there and get a ten of banjo. He was the best runner on a ten of banjo. But he didn't play so long, you know. He was in Baton Rouge, you see. He was in the Blaster and Bricklay, you know. He was good. Did you ever play in Baton Rouge? Did you ever play in Baton Rouge? I've been. Play music there. Oh yeah. I had a job there once, but we couldn't take it on the count of we had so many dates yet and they sent Bob Lyons, but they sent Bob Lyons 75 dollars and they didn't like the way he talked. And so they went back and told me. And so they sent me about $60 and they told me they would get a ban. So they got a ban from Nashville, Mississippi. And they kept him there about 67 years. And they told me a ban. And they said, see, we had a job, we didn't have been there yet. Then they used to go up there and drink dances and play for white and colored people up there. Every now and then they'd get a chance to get them a taste.
Ask him who were some of the bands in Baton Rouge.

Say, who were some of the bands in Baton Rouge? Some of them, well, I didn't know now they got George Williams. You know him George Williams? And uh. Spider used to have a band there, didn't he? Who? Spider. Spider. Oh, Spider, he don't play no more. He was a good corner player, Spider. He don't play no more. Me and him was in Houston, Texas together. Yeah. Yeah, he don't play no more. No. Maybe they say he played a little bit of a job, but not much. Even his daddy used to play, you know. What is Spider's right name? That's the name I know. Spider's no Spider, you see.
That's like Kid Victor. I don't know his right name. Yeah. From Baton Rouge.

And all the rest of them fellas I know, they did. And you say, have a fella there that had a band that played trombone named Stuart. Stuart, yeah, yeah. And then they had a Stuart premiere, used to play trumpet. Yeah. He went up there, but I went up there and played with them a while, you know, until I got ready to come home. He had the Johnson band. Oh, yeah. Yeah.
Well, I wanted to tell you.
Let me see, he had another band. I can't think of the name of it. But only by the days, no, I can't think of it.
Hill City, I think, was up there.
Hill City?
Yeah.

Hill City, say. Yeah, that's old. I went to bed around about three or four years old. And my brother used to play it. My oldest brother. And Walter Burke and that band and Charlie Vidal. You ever heard of Charlie Vidal? Now what did he play? He's a little fella like me. What did he play? He played chord it, clarinet, violin, bass, guitar, any kind of. All around me. Yeah, he was really a professor. And he could play too. And at first I thought he just could play his violin. So I went up there, I was playing manning and I was good, you know. So I said, Charlie was there and I asked my brother, I said, John, can Charlie play manning? He said, wait, I'm going to let you hear it. He said, Charlie, come on. I said, where's the piece from my little kid's brother? And Charlie played that manning and oh, he made me sick. And there was a thing of the girls who played for getting seen. They had a piece called a black and white rag, you know, at that time, you know. May for leaf rag, all that, Charlie would now play all that. And that's I had to take that in package before I could play it, you know. That's a rag I never would have to take it away with it. I don't believe. And there was Walter Birch, he used to play with the Hill City too over there, the tambour, the tambour. We had plenty of brothers. Cornelius, brother named Cornelius, I don't forget his name. And the Piper brothers, they could play.
And get the instruments. What instruments?

I can. You say, what instruments did they play? The Piper, one we played, I played with Klein, one trampone and one guitar. They don't play no more neither. They even, they were dating to my cousin, you know, two miles, you know. Victor and them. Here they come here.
What kind of music did his father play? What kind of music did his father play?
Your father. Oh, uh, my father. Oh, flute and violin, just out of the day.
Did he play any head numbers? Huh?

Play any head numbers? Head numbers? By head. No, he could hear. Because I, you know, that's where the music is five cents a piece then. You don't see music. You don't see much anymore, flute. I bought a piece, you know. I came home and I was running over it, you know. I was running over it. And so, my father say, guys, what you trying to play? I said, oh, papa, you don't know that piece. I said, I just bought that. That's a new piece. He said, play it again? And then that made me play it better, you know. And he went in his trunk, he got that flute, you know, he had lost his line, you know. And he got that flute, he said, oh, yeah. He said, now this means you play. I said, papa, you don't know that piece. He said, you start to play it. I said, papa, you don't know that piece. He said, my granddaddy used to play that piece. He said, yeah, he said, it's new to your but not to me. He said, all them pieces I sit down there and listen to, he said, I can play them all. He said, but sometimes when I really listen to, he said, I couldn't play it right sight. I had to run over it two, three times. And I had to count, you know, to get it together. And that's why he used to tell me, present piece of the year we played, they don't play them, so it's new to us.
Ask him if you remembers the name of that number.

He said, what was the name of that number? The Civil Triad of Montgomery. Ask him any other numbers his father used to play. Say, you remember any other numbers your father used to play? You remember any other numbers your father used to play? Well, you see, he didn't play much. He didn't play much around there. Now and then he would pick his food up. And sometimes he would touch the guitars, just run over it, picking, you know, like that. And he didn't play many pieces, you know. Blues?
Play any blues?
Hmm? Did your father play any blues? No, he didn't know the blues. Did you ever get anything much on Bob Lyons?
No, get him to tell more about Bob.

He said he wants you to talk some more about Bob Lyons. Oh, Bob Lyons? Yeah. Yeah, Bob he said, plenty of kid bands, you know. And, but he was like that crooked. He was like that crooked. Yeah. Yeah. Bob was taking money on the job, you know. And then when we go on the job, you know, we had to come short all the time. Bob didn't get deposit and do spending. And then he said, I'm going to pay you on the next job. Well, then I did. I said, all of us left him, you know. We stayed with him about six or seven months. He was crooked all right. Yeah, yeah.
Who did they have with him?

Who did they have with him then? What he had with him? Yeah. You might know the fellas. I was playing with him at the time. Bonnie, Bonnie Pigar, yeah, him. And his brother, drum, yeah. We were playing together. Alex. Yeah. And then Charlie, Charlie Decanje, he was blowing trumpets. He's up there. Real light fella. Yeah, he's up there, but he don't play. He's a policeman up there now. Where? Where's the policeman at? I believe in Chicago. And, uh, what's the other fella named? Bill Matthews, he was playing drums. Yeah. You know him, eh? Oh, he remember the worst thing. He beat me. Yeah, he's a trombone player now, yeah. He was playing with athletes. But the team now, you know, after he got a new outfit. Oh, Bill Matthews is a lucky fella. Bill Matthews is a lucky fella. Bill Matthews is a lucky fella. Yeah. Yeah. Bill Matthews is a lucky fella. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. He got a wonderful break. Yeah. Well, who played trombone with Bob Lyons? Who played trombone with Bob Lyons? Big Ernie Skelly. Mm-hm.
Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.
Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.
Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.

You know, it was very big, about six feet and so many inches tall, you know. And we had to get all beautiful and put them all in together, you know. So, and I got, me and Ernest went together, you know. And when I met with Ernest's house, Ernest's pants could make me a whole suit. I asked, I said, what make I have to pay the same thing Ernest paid? Ernest take up all that good. He said, well, we have to go through the same thing we do with you, we do with Ernest. I couldn't understand it, you know. He kept six too, he had diabetes, he cut one of his legs off. He went blind, then his eyesight came back, then he cut his other leg off. And after that, he died, you know. He wasn't here when he died, eh? No. He was a good trombone player too.
Ask him if he knew Big Cornish.
Did you know Corny? Who? Big Corny? He's a big little Big Corny. He was another chicken one too. He was about six feet tall too. He was tall. And then she called me and him, Buck and Jeff.
Tell him I heard he had a fight with Corny.

Say, he heard you had a fight with Corny. I think I heard about that. I think it was on my birthday that night, I got drunk, you know. And Tony told me to stop playing, you know. Stop drinking. I said, oh, you ain't got nothing to do with me. I said, the white people, they was giving it to me, helping me to celebrate. And Tony got mad. I said, you big son got busted. I said, go ahead, sit on, sit on, sit on. And then after he told me to come over, you know. Zip would play with his dad, you know. You know Zip, don't you? Kid Vidi, you know them? Yeah. He always would play with me. And let me say, what's the name? Guy Kelly. Guy Kelly. He died in Chicago or New York? Yeah, I played taps for him. Huh? I played taps at his funeral. Oh yeah? In Chicago, huh? Yeah. In Chicago, huh? Yeah. Yeah. In Chicago. Yeah. Yeah. In Chicago. Yeah. He died in Chicago or New York? Yeah, I played taps for him. Huh? I played taps at his funeral. Oh yeah? In Chicago, huh? Yeah. Now Lee, is he living here? Yeah. Yeah, Lee was down there, but he was sick. He's sick now? Yeah, he was something like me. He was constipated. He used to suffer, but I just started to start to be constipated about a week, nine, almost a week. That made me sick so bad, you see. He used to be a sick man before he left here, you know. We used to always try to help him out, you know. And I heard, buddy, I heard that, uh, Lewis Armstrong kept him out there. Yeah, yeah.
Tell him I heard that when Cornish swung at him, he'd run between his legs.
Say, heard that when Cornish swung at you, you'd run between his legs. Yeah.
That's dumb.
I did tell you, I thought that. No, Andy Anderson. Andy Anderson. The trumpet player. The trumpet player.
Andy Anderson, the young fella.
He said, Andy Anderson, the trumpet player is a young fella.
Oh, oh. He told me about it.
He told him about it. Yeah. You know, Anderson? Yeah.
Yeah.

Yeah. I used to play with him too. Emily's cousin, Earl Foster. You never heard of him, eh? Yeah, I know him. That's Anderson's cousin. Yeah. That's a funny story to hear. Tell it, you know. Yeah, after he came up there that night to get me, you know.
Yeah, but he wasn't doing nothing.
He used to come meet me on his job, you know. We'd come home together, you know. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.
Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.

Mm-hm. Kid Allen and Albert Martin, he's there too. You remember that Albedroom? Yeah. And Alex Scott. We had a band there, bass player. We had a band there. That's where, you know, left and went to Mexico, you know. And after that, when we come back, when I got a bass player, he left too. He used to wouldn't go nowhere but right up the country. He's kind of his daddy. Yeah, I remember. Tell me his son is almost as good as him now. Who, Red Allen? Huh? Who, Red Allen? Yeah. You don't know his son, eh? No, I don't know him. That's what they tell me. You know Red Allen? I don't know his son. No, I don't know his son either.
Red Allen has been to Europe with Dude Ori.

Oh, Kid Ori. Oh, yeah. After I'd let Kid Ori to band once with a mandolin, you know. And, you know, like taking a hot lead to bass and the guitar playing by itself. But I wasn't playing guitar then. I was playing mandolin. And the violin player couldn't go, so I wasn't playing. I was playing. And when they stopped, me and Eddie kept playing. And it sounds so good, that's just all of them take a hot now, you see. And they let the piano take a hot. Drum, guitar. And you know, each one of them take a hot, you know.
Ask him who was with Ed Ori.
And Eddie, he's up there yet too, isn't he? With Kid Ori, yeah.
So, ask him? Ask him who was with Ori.

Who was with Ori? Chip Matthews, Stonewall, Johnny Brown, and Johnny Dot. He's there too, yeah. He had. Let me see. He had, let me see. Ask him the instruments too. He was playing drummers. I said, what instrument did they play? What instrument did they play? Well, uh, Chip Matthews played a trumpet. Johnny Dot, Clioness, Kid Ori on the trombone, Eddie Gardner on the bass. And, uh, let me see. Stonewall, you see. Stonewall? Stonewall was on the guitar. And, uh, I believe he had, uh, uh, Martin on drums. Henry Martin? Henry Martin, yeah. All them days now, yeah.
Who was the violin player?
Yeah, he was drumming.
Now, who was the violin player?

Did they have a violin player? No, he was better with a guitar and a piano player. Yeah. Who was the violin player? Who was the violin player? Yeah. I was Koochie Martin. Koochie Martin, oh yeah. Yeah. And that time I met them fellas, I was little kid. You know, when they were playing, I could beat them all playing. They looked like they all went back. Yeah. That's just the way they're young to do with me now, you see. That's right. If I go out, they can beat me playing, you see. Ask him who some of the great musicians had played. He said, who were some of the great musicians from years back? The head men.
The head men.

The head men. The way they used to call them. Peter Hunter. John Rubishow. King Oliver. Louis Armstrong. Fink Martin. You didn't know Buddy Bowling, did you? Yeah, I was a little kid then. Yeah. He stayed at the corner for a while. And one day I was passing and he called me in. And he told me, he said, you drunk brother, isn't he? I said, yes sir. And he said, go down there and get me fifteen cents a beer. And the one time he got him fifteen cents a beer. You know, we used to go there and shoot down, look under the doors and knock, then somebody come and get the bucket. But I carried it there. And he told me to come in. And when I went in, I'm about to run home and told my brother, I said, you little brother's client down there with Kid Bowling. He's in the room. He said, go down there and get me a little time. And knock on the door. And knock on the door. And the brother Bowling comes in the door. He said, hello John. He said, what's your name? He said, buddy, how are you? I come for my little brother. He said, you got to go somewhere else. He said, right there he is. And so he said, they talked a little while. He said, all right, buddy, I see you, Simone. My brother said, all right. He said, you know who that is? I said, no, who is it, John? He said, that's Buddy Bowling. I said, what? That's Buddy Bowling. He said, there's nothing there. That baby died not so long ago. He was another one, Big. Everything was him. Then after him, there was a little fella called Edward Klim. I used to always take Edward Klim for Buddy Bowling. You know. Really? Let me see. Tell that. Buddy Scott, you ever met him? Get up there. So you ever met Buddy Scott?
Don't know him.
Oh, you don't know him. I heard him. Buddy Christian, you ever met him?
He passed about nine months ago. Yeah, what is it?
He passed. So he died about nine months ago.
Oh, yeah. I didn't know him. Well, I went to New York about three months ago. Yeah.
Oh, yeah. He never did come back yet. But me and him both, we used to go down to live as a young girl. Yeah.

Yeah, did they give you an x-ray down there? Where down? Hospital. Oh yeah. Yeah. But they said they didn't find nothing down there. They said it wasn't the matter with my lungs. Well, they're talking about two months to find something on me. Yeah. They laid me all kinds of ways down there. Yeah. Alright.
Let's ask you about Buddy Christian again.

You want to talk about Buddy Christian again? Oh, Buddy Christian? Yeah, we used to go around them little girls, and he used to have stock of music, and he'd make them little girls play it. And after they played, they'd make them play it again. Then he'd sit down and catch in the same key. And he couldn't read the tone, you know. But he'd catch it in the same key, and that made everybody think he could read. But people that know music know that he made the right chords, you know, when he was playing. But that's where I used to catch them too, you know. Yeah.
Ask him who his favorite trombone players were in those days, way back.

He said, who was your favorite trombone player way back in those days? Who was the? Your favorite trombone player. Who was the best one? Yeah, your favorite. Oh, you know, I see. I left before I could play music good. It's, uh, let me see. Rob Palmer, did you say you know him? He's living there, you say? In Chicago.
In Chicago.

For him and then Duke. You know Duke? Zoo the Duke. Zoot? Yeah, trombone player. Yeah, yeah. Then set up a rule. Earl Humper. Harrison over the river, you know. And Yankee, he's there too. Yeah. And there's another trombone player over there. I said, this is man. Who did he play with? Kid Thomas. You know Kid Thomas? Yeah, you should play with him over there. Louie Nelson lives with him now. Louie Nelson? Huh? Louie Nelson? Louie Nelson? He's with Kid Thomas now. No, Louie Nelson was the clownette there. No, he's from— did you the clownette there? Tell them them. No. No. No. No.
No.
No.
No. No. No. No. No. No.

He said, this is Dr. Nelson's song. Oh, I used to play Louie Nelson and George Nelson. One played trampone and one played saxophone. Yeah, me and Louie, we used to play together a long time. It was Kit Harris then when we were playing together.
Who was Kit Harris?

He played just there. Kit Harris? Who was him? Huh? Kit Harris, I didn't know him. No, you didn't know Kit Harris? No, he did too, Kit Harris. Yeah, trumpet, yeah. Me and Louie and George used to play with Kit Harris. He's a good trampone player, Louie Nelson did.
Who was the main player?
I thought you were talking about the other Louie Nelson, flying up players, saxophone.
Who else was there?
See, there's a dine time somewhere. The youth, I don't know if it is, yes, you know. See, who else was in the band?
With Kit Harris.
With Kit Harris. Well, I think me, Louie, George, and I played a girlfriend.
On piano?
No, I mean Kit Harris' girlfriend, you know.

segments.title: Recording setup and introductions at Little Dad's home
segments.summary: Allen sets the date (17 Nov 1959) and address; Punch Miller and Little Dad give their names and nicknames.

segments.title: Selling sheet music for Piron and Williams
segments.summary: Asked about the Tulane Avenue publishing shop, he says he sold their sheet music on trips for ten cents to musicians and fifteen to others, without playing with them then.

segments.chapter: Mexico trip and Charlie Tolles band
segments.title: Trip to Mexico in 1926
segments.summary: He went to Mexico in 1926 for three and a half months with Charlie Tolles's band, played with a white band under Professor Connett and a small four-piece group, then returned to his job.

segments.chapter: Mexico trip and Charlie Tolles band
segments.title: Joe Oliver and the early Kid band
segments.summary: He knew Joe Oliver, older by five or six years, who came up in a youngsters' brass band and later led his own; he recalls Oliver's wife Stella and Armstrong leaving with him.

segments.chapter: Mexico trip and Charlie Tolles band
segments.title: Who was in Charlie Tolles's band for Mexico
segments.summary: Tolles's band backed out of Mexico, so he grabbed whoever he could; Little Dad played drums and piano, the group played Charleston and mixed with Mexican bands.

segments.chapter: Baton Rouge, Hill City and family music
segments.title: Switching from guitar to banjo and Baton Rouge players
segments.summary: He started on guitar at about 21-22, stayed on guitar and then banjo, refused to change at first, and mentions rival banjoists, George Foster and a Baton Rouge job lost over Bob Lyons.

segments.chapter: Baton Rouge, Hill City and family music
segments.title: Bands in Baton Rouge and the Hill City band
segments.summary: Asked about Baton Rouge bands he names George Williams, Spider, Stuart, and the Hill City band with Charlie Vidal, his brother John and Walter Burke.

segments.chapter: Baton Rouge, Hill City and family music
segments.title: His father's flute and violin playing
segments.summary: His father played flute and violin by ear; a story about his father recognizing a new piece shows the repertoire was old; no blues.

segments.chapter: Bob Lyons band and New Orleans musicians
segments.title: Bob Lyons, his crooked band and its members
segments.summary: He describes bandleader Bob Lyons as crooked with money, lists sidemen (Bonnie Pigar, Charlie Decanje, Bill Matthews) and a big trombonist who lost both legs.

segments.chapter: Bob Lyons band and New Orleans musicians
segments.title: Big Cornish, a fight and old friends
segments.summary: Talk about Big Corny, a drunken birthday quarrel, Guy Kelly's funeral, Andy Anderson and a band with Kid Allen and Alex Scott before Mexico.

segments.chapter: Early heroes and Kid Ory band
segments.title: Playing with Kid Ory's band and its members
segments.summary: He once sat in with Kid Ory's band on mandolin and lists its men: Chip Matthews, Stonewall, Johnny Dot, Eddie Gardner, Henry Martin and Koochie Martin.

segments.chapter: Early heroes and Kid Ory band
segments.title: Head men of early jazz and Buddy Bolden
segments.summary: He names the early head men and tells how as a boy he fetched beer for Buddy Bolden; briefly mentions Buddy Christian's death.

segments.chapter: Early heroes and Kid Ory band
segments.title: Hospital aside and Buddy Christian faking reading
segments.summary: After an aside about his x-ray, he says Buddy Christian had girls play pieces, then caught the key by ear so everyone thought he could read.

segments.title: Favorite trombonists and Kit Harris's band
segments.summary: He names early trombone players, then Louie and George Nelson, who played with Kit Harris's band with George Williams and bassist Richard McLean.

segments.title: Frankie Dusen's band and Joe Howard
segments.summary: He recalls Frankie Dusen's band with trumpeter Joe Howard, who later played tuba, and where Dusen lived and what he played.

segments.title: Clarinet players, barrel house clarinettists and George Lewis
segments.summary: He names good clarinettists (Bechet, Picou, McCurdy), barrel house players, George Lewis, and the Bond brothers.

segments.title: Trumpet players and plunger mute specialists
segments.summary: Favorite trumpeters include Oliver, Guy Kelly and Buddy Petit; Chris Kelly was best with the plunger mute.

segments.title: Early guitar players and Rabbit from James Alley
segments.summary: He names early guitarists, praises fingerpicker Henry Roy, and describes Rabbit from James Alley who sang and played guitar.

segments.title: Hennessy song, Geddes and Morris, and funny songs
segments.summary: Allen asks about songs on Chief Hennessy and a wagon song; he recalls songs on Geddes and Morris, and Armstrong's funny songs.

segments.title: Drummers and following parades as a boy
segments.summary: He lists good drummers (Black Happy, Black Benny, Snag) and recalls following parades as a boy before he could play.

segments.title: Good bass players and Snags Jones
segments.summary: He names bass players (Fulston, Scott, T-Boy) and discusses drummer Clifford Jones, known as Snag.

segments.title: Other drummers and bandleader Lovington
segments.summary: Talk of drummers like Zutty Singleton, a Chicago drummer, and a classical trumpeter-bandleader Lovington, linked to Charlie Love.

segments.title: Putting heads on his own banjo and Bunk Johnson
segments.summary: He fixed banjo heads himself, sometimes using drum heads, and recalls Bunk driving a float and buying beer.

segments.title: Money and serenading with white patrons
segments.summary: He explains serenading pay: sometimes paid, sometimes food and drink from white people who took them out until daylight.

segments.title: Playing around Franklin and Iberville and the dog house
segments.summary: He played in the French Quarter district, the dog house and other spots around Franklin and Iberville, until about seven or eight years earlier.

segments.title: Band at the Tuxedo and the 25, and clubs like Rice's
segments.summary: He worked with John Kazman and a small unnamed band (Alcee, T-Ball, Albert Fernandez), and talks of Rice's and the Entertainers clubs.

segments.title: Piano players: Tony Jackson, Roscoe Williams, Fats Pichon
segments.summary: He names good pianists, Tony Jackson's songs, blues pianist Roscoe Williams, and Walter 'Fats' Pichon.

segments.title: Recafo the gambler and Little Dad's origin
segments.summary: Allen asks about gambler Recafo; Little Dad says he came to New Orleans after the army and was raised where he was born.

segments.title: Mandolin and violin players, and the Humphreys
segments.summary: He names mandolin and violin players including Jim Humphrey, Johnny Delpy, Peter Bocage and Mario Minelli.

segments.title: Homemade instruments, Leo Watson and old neighbors
segments.summary: Allen asks about washboard and jug players; talk drifts to Leo Watson, where Little Dad lived on St. Peter, and Joe Robichaux.

segments.title: Funerals then and now, Sammy Dutrey and Honore Dutrey
segments.summary: He says funeral jobs have changed, and discusses Eureka musicians Black Happy, Sammy Dutrey and Honore Dutrey's lung trouble.

segments.title: Lewis Dumaine, Gus Metcalf band and the Hall brothers
segments.summary: He describes cornetist Lewis Dumaine, the band with Edmond Hall and others, and Hall's brothers Robert and Herbert.

segments.title: Closing thanks
segments.summary: Allen says they will return; thanks and goodbyes.
